prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute post-stroke cognitive impairment to depression without formal assessment
Do not read the chronic petechial haemorrhagic transformation as a new haemorrhage and stop the antiplatelet
Do not dismiss a symptomatic 50-69% stenosis as below the threshold for revascularisation
Do not defer secondary prevention until cognition is 'settled'; recurrent stroke is the main risk to cognition
Do not certify fitness to drive on the strength of motor recovery when attentional neglect is documented
Do not prescribe anticholinergic or sedating medications during cognitive rehabilitation
required_recommendations: Refer the symptomatic 50-60% right ICA stenosis to the vascular team without delay for a decision on carotid endarterectomy: the stroke was ten weeks ago and the benefit falls with time [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]
Continue clopidogrel 75 mg; the chronic petechial haemorrhagic transformation is not a reason to stop it [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]
Lower blood pressure (148/84 mmHg) gradually to below 130/80 mmHg, checking orthostatic BP at each change [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]

Intensify lipid lowering to LDL below 55 mg/dL (current 78 mg/dL on rosuvastatin 20 mg): very high risk after an atherosclerotic ischaemic stroke at 75 with hypertension and diabetes; add ezetimibe or increase to rosuvastatin 40 mg [ACC_AHA_dyslipidemia_2026]
Individualise the HbA1c target to about below 8.0% and avoid hypoglycaemia; HbA1c 7.9% on metformin [ADA_older_adults_2026]
Refer for cognitive rehabilitation, keep him off the road until the formal driving assessment given the left-sided inattention, and plan cognitive reassessment because the trajectory can still change

avoided_actions.rationale: No episodes, fluctuation or progressive course; EEG has no diagnostic role in a deficit dated to a documented stroke.
No spontaneous parkinsonism, fluctuations, hallucinations or dream enactment; a dopamine transporter scan does not address the question.
No feature of Lewy body disease or autonomic failure; cardiac sympathetic imaging does not inform this diagnosis.
A deficit dated to a documented stroke, not a subacute progressive syndrome: an untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune battery has no indication.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes.
A transthoracic echocardiogram at the stroke admission ten weeks ago was normal, and an ipsilateral carotid stenosis is the likely mechanism; repeating it would not change management.
72 hours of telemetry at the admission showed sinus rhythm and the infarct lies downstream of an ipsilateral stenosis; prolonged monitoring would not change management.

accepted: Post-stroke vascular dementia following a right middle cerebral artery superior division infarct, on a background of pre-existing moderate small-vessel disease
major neurocognitive disorder due to vascular disease

differential.key_features: Common at ten weeks and a genuine confounder, but he denies low mood, GDS-15 is 4/15, he engages with rehabilitation, and the deficit is attentional and executive with objective left-sided omissions
Alertness is stable with no fluctuation, no new medication and no infective or metabolic trigger

differential.diagnosis: Alzheimer's disease unmasked by the stroke
differential.key_features: There is no premorbid history of cognitive decline, the hippocampi are preserved, and recall is cue-responsive; a biomarker would be required to raise this and nothing in the presentation calls for it

differential.diagnosis: Expected early post-stroke cognitive recovery trajectory
differential.key_features: Cognitive deficits at ten weeks may still improve, which is why the diagnosis is dated from the event and reassessed — but the functional impairment now is real and requires management now
No fluctuation, hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism or dream enactment

key_clinical_evidence: Post-stroke dementia is diagnosed on the temporal criterion: cognitive decline beginning within three months of a documented stroke, with a deficit that the lesion can explain
Motor and cognitive recovery dissociate after stroke, and a good NIHSS improvement says nothing about executive function
Pre-existing small-vessel disease lowers cognitive reserve and helps explain why a single infarct produced a dementia in this patient
Chronic petechial haemorrhagic transformation after thrombolysis is expected and is not a reason to withdraw antiplatelet therapy
Cognitive deficits at ten weeks can still evolve, so the diagnosis carries a reassessment plan rather than being treated as fixed

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Petechial haemorrhagic transformation within a thrombolysed infarct is chronic and expected; it does not contraindicate secondary-prevention antiplatelet therapy
red_herrings.intended_effect: Read as a new intracerebral haemorrhage, prompting withdrawal of antiplatelet therapy

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Motor and cognitive recovery dissociate; the attentional and executive deficits with objective left-sided omissions map onto the frontoparietal infarct and have not tracked the motor improvement
red_herrings.data_point: Good motor recovery from NIHSS 12 to 3
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests the stroke has largely resolved and that the cognitive complaints must be functional or depressive

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Pietro Lombardi is a 75-year-old retired site manager who had a right middle cerebral artery infarct ten weeks ago, thrombolysed with a fall in NIHSS from 12 to 3. His motor recovery has been good: he walks with a stick and uses the left hand for gross tasks. His wife's concern is different. Since discharge he has not been able to resume anything requiring organisation: he cannot follow the sequence of his own medication, has twice set out for the pharmacy and returned without going in, and cannot manage the household bills he handled until the day of the stroke. He loses the thread of a conversation with two other people present, misses objects on his left in the kitchen, and does not seem fully aware of the extent of his difficulties. He remembers events when reminded of the context. There has been slow improvement in the motor deficit over ten weeks with no corresponding improvement in the organisational difficulty. He denies low mood, sleeps adequately and engages with rehabilitation willingly. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation in alertness and no dream enactment. His blood pressure at discharge and since has been in the 145-155 range.
